stem:
Study Sources A to D and answer both questions. The topic is the causes of the French Revolution.

**Source A** — a list of complaints from the inhabitants of a fictional village in Anjou, March 1789 (invented for this question)

> The people of this parish humbly ask that the king reduce the salt tax and the taille, and that the nobles and clergy pay their share. They ask that the lord's dues and the tithe be lessened, that the roads be repaired and that the Estates-General meet regularly. They declare themselves faithful subjects of a king whom they believe to be the father of his people.

**Source B** — a letter from a fictional printer in Paris to his brother in Lyon, in July of that year (invented for this question)

> Bread has not been so dear in my lifetime. My workshop has little work, for the nobles who bought our books have left town. The Assembly at Versailles gives us hope, but the king has brought soldiers around the city, and men say that Monsieur Necker is dismissed. The people believe there is a plot to starve us, and many speak of buying powder and muskets.

**Source C** — a private memorandum by a fictional royal finance official, written before the Assembly of Notables met (invented for this question)

> The treasury is empty and the debt grows each year. Interest alone takes nearly half of all that we collect. The only remedy is a tax on land that all must pay, whether noble, priest or commoner. The Notables will not accept this, for they are themselves the owners of the land. Unless they agree, the king must call the nation's representatives.

**Source D** — a cartoon of the kind published in France at the time, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> The cartoon shows an old peasant bent beneath a heavy load, with a priest and a noble riding on his back. A stone at his feet is marked with the word Estates. In the distance dark clouds gather above a palace.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Compare Sources A and B as evidence about the problems facing ordinary French people. [15]

points.description: Similarities: both show hardship and anxiety about the cost of living (the taxes in A, the price of bread in B)
Both look to the representatives at Versailles to bring improvement
Differences: A is rural and concerns taxes, dues and tithe; B is urban and concerns bread, unemployment and fear of soldiers
Attitude to the king: A expresses loyalty; B shows distrust and the belief in a plot after Necker's dismissal
Provenance: A is a petition for the king, formal and perhaps guided by a lawyer; B is a private letter and so frank
Context and own knowledge: the salt tax, tithe and dues; the bad harvest of 1788; Necker's dismissal on 11 July

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The sources agree that ordinary people were suffering and that they hoped for change from Versailles. Source A, from a village in March, complains of the salt tax, the taille, the lord's dues and the tithe, and asks that nobles and clergy pay their share. Source B, from Paris in July, says that bread has never been so dear and that work has dried up. Both therefore describe a burden that fell on the Third Estate, and both look to the assembly for relief: A asks that the Estates-General meet regularly, and B says that the Assembly gives hope.

They differ in the kind of problem and the attitude to the king. A is rural and concerned with taxes and feudal obligations; B is urban and concerned with hunger, unemployment and fear. A expresses loyalty to a king who is the father of his people, but B, written after the dismissal of Necker and the movement of troops, fears that the king may side with the nobles and that there is a plot to starve the people. The difference is partly a matter of date: A was written in the spring when hopes were high, and B in July after the crisis had grown.

Provenance explains much of this. A is a list of complaints prepared for the king, in a formal style, and probably drafted with the help of a local lawyer; its loyalty may be conventional and its aim is to persuade. B is a private letter to a brother, so the writer has no reason to be anything but frank, although he reports rumour. Own knowledge supports both: the cahiers did complain of the salt tax, tithe and dues, the harvest of 1788 had been poor, and Necker was dismissed on 11 July. The two sources are therefore good evidence for different parts of the same crisis, rural grievance against privilege and urban fear of hunger, and are more useful together than separately.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A to D support the view that the financial crisis was the main cause of the outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789? Use the sources and your own knowledge. [25]

points.description: Support: Source C shows the debt, the interest burden and the failure of the Notables, which forced the call for an Estates-General
Support: Source A shows the tax grievances that the crisis made worse
Challenge: Source B shows hunger and fear of a plot as immediate causes beyond finance
Challenge: Source D shows privilege and the unequal estates as a deeper cause
Own knowledge: Calonne, the Assembly of Notables, the American war, the harvest of 1788, the voting dispute, the Enlightenment
Provenance and weighing: C is a private official view; A is a petition; B a private letter; D a cartoon with a purpose
A supported judgement about how far finance was the main cause

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The sources give considerable support to the view that the financial crisis was the main cause of the Revolution, but they also show that other causes mattered.

Source C gives the strongest support. It is a private memorandum by a finance official, and it says that the treasury is empty, that interest takes nearly half of revenue, and that only a tax on all landowners can solve the problem. Because it was private, it is likely to be frank, and it agrees with what we know: the American war had added greatly to the debt, Calonne's land tax was refused by the Assembly of Notables in 1787, and this led to the calling of the Estates-General. The source also shows that the privileged blocked reform. Source A supports the financial theme from the other side: the villagers complain of the salt tax, the taille, the dues and the tithe and want nobles and clergy to pay their share. The unfairness of the tax system was at the heart of the crisis, though A is a petition addressed to the king and may be conventional in its loyalty.

The sources also challenge the view. Source B shows that in July the immediate concern in Paris was hunger and fear of a plot. The harvest of 1788 had been poor, bread was dear, and the king's troops and Necker's dismissal frightened people into action. These were triggers rather than finance. Source D, a cartoon, presents the peasant carrying a priest and a noble: it points to a deeper cause in the unequal estates and privilege, and to resentment, but as a cartoon it is designed to provoke and cannot show how widely it was shared. Neither B nor D mentions the debt.

Own knowledge widens the picture. The financial crisis forced the king to call the Estates-General, but what turned it into a revolution was the dispute over voting, the leadership of the bourgeoisie, the ideas of the Enlightenment and the king's use of troops. Without hunger and the events of July, the Revolution might have been a constitutional reform.

Overall, the sources support the view to a large extent that finance was the main cause of the crisis, since it is the cause that made the old system unable to continue and that is common to C and A. But it was not the sole cause of the Revolution: privilege, hunger and political mistakes explain why the crisis became a revolution. I conclude that the financial crisis was the most important underlying cause, though it needed these other factors to produce the events of 1789.

stem:
Study Sources A to D and answer both questions. The topic is the Terror.

**Source A** — a report by a fictional representative on mission to the Committee of Public Safety, November 1793 (invented for this question)

> I found the department in revolt and the grain hidden. By arresting the hoarders and the leaders of the rising I have restored order within a week. The prisons are full, but the army has bread and the roads are open. Severity is the only means to save the Republic from its enemies, inside and out.

**Source B** — a letter from a fictional provincial widow to her sister, the following spring (invented for this question)

> My husband was arrested because a neighbour said he had spoken against the Maximum. He had done no more than complain of the price of candles. The prison is crowded and we are told nothing. Everyone is afraid to speak, and we wonder who will be denounced next.

**Source C** — a petition from a fictional section of Paris to the Convention, in September of that year (invented for this question)

> The enemies of the Republic are everywhere: hoarders, priests who will not swear and officers who betray us. We ask that firm measures be taken, that suspects be arrested and that the price of bread be fixed. Without this the Republic will fall to the foreign kings.

**Source D** — a print of the kind sold in Paris at the time, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> The print shows a crowd in a Paris square watching a guillotine on a platform. Soldiers stand in a line around it, and children play at the edge of the crowd. Above the scene a banner reads: The Republic, one and indivisible.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Compare Sources A and B as evidence about the effects of the Terror. [15]

points.description: Similarities: both show that arrests filled the prisons and both concern grain, prices or the Maximum
Both show that fear and suspicion were widespread
Differences: A is the official view that severity brought order and bread; B is the victim's view of arbitrary arrest
A concerns the army and the Republic's survival; B concerns the family and injustice
Provenance: A is an official report to justify his own conduct; B is a private letter from a victim's family, emotional and partial
Context and own knowledge: the Law of Suspects of September 1793, representatives on mission, denunciations, the Maximum

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Both sources show that the Terror filled the prisons and spread fear, and both are concerned with food and prices. In Source A the representative arrests hoarders and leaders of a revolt, admitting that the prisons are full, and in Source B the widow's husband has been arrested for a remark on the Maximum, and the prison is crowded. Both therefore illustrate the wide use of arrest under the Law of Suspects.

They differ in their view of its effects. A is an official report that presents severity as successful: order has been restored in a week, the army has bread and the roads are open. B is the account of a victim's family: the arrest was for a trivial complaint, nobody is told anything, and everybody is afraid of denunciation. A therefore stresses necessity and results, B stresses arbitrariness and injustice. A looks at the survival of the Republic, B at one family.

Provenance explains the difference. A was written by a representative reporting to the Committee, who had every reason to show that his harsh methods worked, and who is writing from the viewpoint of a man with power. B is a private letter to a sister, written in distress by someone who had lost a husband; she is likely to be honest about her feelings but cannot know the reasons for the arrest. Own knowledge supports both: representatives on mission had wide powers, the Law of Suspects of September 1793 allowed arrest of people merely suspected, and denunciations by neighbours were common. The two sources show the same system from opposite sides, and are best used together.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A to D support the view that the Terror was necessary to defend the Republic? Use the sources and your own knowledge. [25]

points.description: Support: Source A (order restored, the army fed) and Source C (enemies everywhere, the demand for firm measures)
Support: Source D suggests public acceptance and the language of the Republic
Challenge: Source B shows arbitrary arrests for trivial remarks, which went beyond defence
Challenge: Source D could also show the spectacle of executions; and the provenance of A and C shows that they have an interest
Own knowledge: foreign invasion, the Vendée and federalist revolts, hunger; but the Great Terror followed Fleurus
Provenance and weighing of the sources
A supported judgement on whether the Terror was necessary

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The sources give some support to the view that the Terror was necessary, but they also suggest that it went further than defence required.

Source A supports the view. The representative claims that firm action restored order in a week, that the grain is released, that the army has bread and that the roads are open. If true, the Terror helped to feed and equip the army, which was essential in 1793. Source C, a petition from a Paris section, says that enemies are everywhere and that the Republic will fall to the foreign kings unless suspects are arrested and the price of bread is fixed. It reflects the view of the sans-culottes, who pressed for emergency measures. These agree with what we know: in 1793 France faced invasion by a coalition, the revolt of the Vendée, the federalist risings and hunger, and the Convention believed that survival required strong government. Source D, a print of an execution under a banner of the Republic, one and indivisible, can be read as showing public acceptance of the measures in the name of unity.

However, other evidence challenges the view. Source B shows a man arrested for a trivial complaint about the price of candles, in a prison where no one is told anything. This suggests arbitrary action, driven by denunciation, which could hardly defend the Republic. It also fits what we know of the Law of Suspects, which allowed arrest on vague grounds. Source D, with children at the edge of the crowd, may suggest that executions had become a spectacle. The reliability of the supporting sources is also limited: A is by a man who must justify his actions, and C by a section that wanted tougher measures, so each had an interest.

Own knowledge confirms both sides. The emergency of 1793 was real, and the army was strengthened by the levée en masse and by Carnot's organisation. But the Terror reached its height in June and July 1794, after the victory at Fleurus had eased the danger, and the Law of 22 Prairial removed safeguards for the accused. This suggests that factional fear and ideology, not only necessity, kept it going. Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor was followed by an end to the system without the loss of the Republic.

On balance, the sources support the view that the Terror was necessary in its early phase, from the spring to the autumn of 1793, when the Republic was in danger. They do not support the claim that it was necessary in its later phase or in its arbitrary forms, as Source B and the events after Fleurus show. I conclude that the Terror was partly necessary, but that it was extended beyond what defence required.

parts.stem: Explain why Calonne's attempt to reform the finances failed. [10]

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Calonne failed because he asked the privileged to give up their exemptions. By 1786 the debt was very large, partly because of the American war, and the tax system fell most heavily on the Third Estate while the nobles and clergy paid little. Calonne proposed a land tax on all owners, whether noble, clergy or commoner, and the end of internal customs barriers.

He knew that the parlements would resist, so he called an Assembly of Notables, hand-picked nobles, clergy and officials, in February 1787. But the Notables were the very people who would pay the tax, and they refused. They said that the tax needed the consent of the nation's representatives and that only an Estates-General could agree it. Calonne was dismissed in April 1787. The failure was important because it showed that the privileged would block reform, and because it left the king to call the Estates-General, which had not met since 1614. It turned a financial problem into a political one.

The financial crisis forced the calling of the Estates-General and the Assembly of Notables made the problem political

Alternative: the Enlightenment, Sieyès and the example of America
Alternative: the bad harvest of 1788 and hunger, the Réveillon riots, the Great Fear
Alternative: the voting dispute, the Tennis Court Oath, the king's use of troops and the Bastille turned crisis into revolution

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The financial crisis was the most important cause of the outbreak of the Revolution, but it needed other factors to turn crisis into revolution, so I agree to a large extent but not entirely.

The financial crisis explains why the monarchy could not carry on as before. The state was heavily in debt, particularly because of the American war, and interest took roughly half of royal spending. The tax system was unfair and inefficient, with exemptions for the privileged. Turgot, Necker and Calonne all tried to reform it and failed because the privileged and the parlements blocked them. After the Notables refused Calonne's land tax in 1787, the crown had no alternative but to call the Estates-General. Without the financial crisis there would have been no meeting of the Estates-General, and so no National Assembly. It was thus the direct cause of the political crisis.

Other factors were also important. Privilege and social resentment created grievances: the cahiers show peasants complaining of dues, the tithe and the salt tax, and the bourgeoisie resenting its exclusion from power. The Enlightenment gave educated people ideas of rights and the sovereignty of the people, and Sieyès argued in January 1789 that the Third Estate was the nation. The American war showed that a republic could be founded. These helped to make people unwilling to accept a return to the old order. The bad harvest of 1788, which made bread dear in the spring and summer of 1789, brought hunger and riots such as the Réveillon riots, and a fear of plots which fed the Great Fear.

Finally, the course of events mattered. The dispute about voting by order or head, the Tennis Court Oath, the king's use of troops and the dismissal of Necker, and the storming of the Bastille on 14 July turned a reform movement into a revolution. Many historians believe that if the king had accepted voting by head or acted differently the outcome might have been a constitutional monarchy.

In comparing the factors, the financial crisis is the most important because it was the necessary condition: it created the opportunity and forced the king to call representatives. But it was not sufficient: the grievances and ideas gave the Third Estate its purpose, and the political mistakes of 1789 decided that the result would be a revolution. I conclude that the financial crisis was the main cause of the crisis of 1787-89, but the revolution itself resulted from a combination of factors.

hints: Explain a chain of causes in (a). In (b), weigh finance against privilege, ideas, hunger and the events of 1789.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The flight damaged the monarchy because it showed that the king did not accept the Revolution. On the night of 20-21 June 1791 Louis XVI and his family left Paris in disguise for the eastern frontier, and he left behind a declaration condemning the reforms. This made it clear that he had accepted the Constitution only under pressure.

He was recognised and stopped at Varennes and brought back to Paris. The Assembly claimed that he had been abducted, so as to preserve the constitutional monarchy, but few believed it, and trust in him as a constitutional monarch collapsed. For the first time many people, including some in the Jacobin clubs, began to talk of a republic, which led to the petition at the Champ de Mars in July. The flight also encouraged émigrés and foreign monarchs, who saw the king as a prisoner, and so made war more likely. It was thus a turning point in the loss of the monarchy's authority.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
War was the most important reason why France became a republic by 1792, since it created the crisis in which the monarchy fell, but it acted on earlier weaknesses that the king himself had created, so I agree to a large extent.

War turned a political quarrel into an emergency. The Girondins believed that war would spread the Revolution and expose the king's loyalty, and the king hoped for defeat, and France declared war on Austria in April 1792. The army suffered early defeats, and Prussia joined Austria. In July the Brunswick Manifesto threatened Paris with destruction if the royal family was harmed, and when it was published it convinced many Parisians that the king was in league with the invaders. On 10 August the Paris sections and the fédérés attacked the Tuileries, the Assembly suspended the king and called a Convention, which abolished the monarchy in September. Without the war there would have been no such crisis.

However, the king's conduct had already weakened the monarchy. He used his veto on laws against émigrés and refractory priests, and the flight to Varennes in June 1791 showed that he did not accept the Constitution. After it, many people called for a republic, and the shooting of petitioners at the Champ de Mars deepened the division on the left. The Civil Constitution of the Clergy had divided Catholics and given the counter-revolution a cause, so that many saw the king as sympathetic to enemies of the Revolution.

Other factors were the role of political groups: the Girondins pressed for war, and the sans-culottes of Paris, angry about hunger and suspicious of the king, supplied the force on 10 August.

I conclude that war was the decisive reason, as it made the king's position impossible and brought the people of Paris to act, but it did so because the king had already lost trust through his own actions and the divisions of 1790-91. A republic was not planned in 1789; it was the result of this combination.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Committee introduced the Terror because the Republic seemed in danger of destruction. After the king's execution in January 1793 France was at war with Britain, Spain, the Dutch Republic, Austria and Prussia, and the army suffered defeats; in April General Dumouriez deserted to the enemy.

At home, the call for recruits provoked the revolt in the Vendée in March 1793, and cities such as Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux rose against the Convention. Inflation and hunger meant that the sans-culottes demanded price controls and action against hoarders and traitors, and the Convention responded with the Maximum. Fear of traitors led to the Revolutionary Tribunal and the Law of Suspects of September 1793, which allowed wide arrests. The Committee, reorganised in July 1793 with Robespierre, used these tools to control the provinces and mobilise the nation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
I agree to a large extent that the Directory failed, though it had some successes, because it never won the loyalty of the people and survived only through the army and coups.

Its failures were serious. The Constitution of the Year III was designed to avoid dictatorship, but it produced a government without secure support. Elections often returned deputies whom the Directors disliked, whether royalists in 1797 or Jacobins in 1798, so the Directors cancelled the results, with the help of the army, as at 18 Fructidor in September 1797. This made the regime dependent on force. Corruption and favouritism, associated with Barras, discredited it. The franchise was narrow, and the memory of the Terror and the hunger of the early years left the people indifferent. Financially, the assignats had collapsed and the repudiation of two thirds of the debt in 1797 amounted to a bankruptcy. In 1799 France suffered defeats in Italy and Switzerland and faced a Second Coalition, while Bonaparte was in Egypt. By that year many leaders, such as Sieyès, wanted a new constitution.

Nevertheless, the Directory had achievements. It won victories: Bonaparte's campaigns in Italy ended with the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797, and conquered lands brought money. The currency was stabilised after the end of the assignat, and the state's finances improved somewhat. The Directory survived four years against royalist and Jacobin threats: it crushed the royalist rising of Vendémiaire with the help of Bonaparte, and the Conspiracy of the Equals under Babeuf in 1796. It also restored some local administration.

Comparing these, the successes were mainly military and financial, and depended on the army and on conquest; the failures were political and structural. A regime that has to cancel elections cannot be called well governed. I conclude that the Directory was a failure in its main task of creating a stable constitutional government, though not a total one, since it preserved the Republic and a measure of order until the coup of Brumaire.

parts.stem: Explain why Napoleon Bonaparte was able to seize power in 1799. [10]

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Napoleon was able to seize power because the Directory had lost the support of the people. It depended on the army and coups, was seen as corrupt and had suffered defeats in 1799. Many people wanted order and a government that could end the war.

Napoleon had a great reputation. His victories in Italy in 1796-97 and the Treaty of Campo Formio had made him a national hero, and he used propaganda, including newspapers for the army and France, to build his image. Although the Egyptian expedition had failed, his reports made it seem a success, and he returned in October 1799. Politicians such as Sieyès, a Director, wanted to change the constitution and needed a general to support them. In the coup of 18 Brumaire (9 November 1799) soldiers led by Murat and Napoleon's brother Lucien, president of the Council of Five Hundred, cleared the councils, and little resistance followed. The weakness of the regime and Napoleon's reputation together made the seizure of power possible.

parts.stem: 'The Russian campaign of 1812 was the main reason for Napoleon's fall.' How far do you agree? [20]

The Peninsular War: guerrilla warfare and Wellington tied down large forces from 1808
Nationalism, Leipzig, the capture of Paris in 1814 and allied unity at Chaumont
Napoleon's mistakes and loss of support at home
A comparative judgement on the importance of Russia

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The invasion of Russia was the most important reason for Napoleon's fall because it destroyed his army and encouraged his enemies, but it was linked to other causes, so I agree to a large extent.

In June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia with the Grande Armée of over half a million men, including allies. The Russians retreated and burned supplies, and although Napoleon entered Moscow in September, the Tsar refused to make peace. The retreat in the winter, with hunger, disease and attacks, destroyed most of the army. This was a loss that he could not make good, and it persuaded Prussia and Austria to join Russia and Britain in 1813, which led to his defeat at Leipzig in October 1813 and the invasion of France.

But Russia was itself a result of other causes. The Continental System, which was supposed to ruin Britain, hurt France and its allies, and Russia left it in 1810, which was why Napoleon invaded. The Peninsular War, from 1808, tied down large French forces for years against Spanish guerrillas and Wellington's army, and drained men and money, so that fewer experienced troops were available in 1812. Nationalism grew in Germany and Spain, where conscription, taxes and foreign rule made French rule hated. After Leipzig the allies agreed at Chaumont in 1814 to stay united, entered Paris on 31 March and forced his abdication. Finally, his own mistakes, such as invading Spain and Russia and refusing peace terms in 1813, and the loss of support in France, also contributed.

Comparing causes, the Russian campaign was decisive because it turned a long struggle into a defeat: after 1812 he faced a united Europe with a smaller army. The Peninsular War weakened him earlier but he could have survived it. The Continental System was the root of both wars. I conclude that Russia was the main reason, but that it cannot be separated from the policies that led to it and the nationalism and alliance that finished him.

stem: Evaluate the view that the weakness of the Liberal governments, rather than the strength of the Fascists, was the main reason why Mussolini became prime minister in 1922. [30]

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The weakness of the Liberal governments, and the decisions of the King and the elites that went with it, were more important than the strength of the Fascists in explaining Mussolini's appointment, though weakness alone would not have produced it without the violence and pressure of the Fascist movement.

The Liberal state was weak in several ways. The system of proportional representation produced chambers in which the Socialists, the Catholic Popular Party and the Liberals could not form a stable majority, and governments fell quickly: Nitti, Giolitti, Bonomi and Facta between 1919 and 1922. The Liberals had no mass party. Giolitti made things worse in 1921 when he brought the Fascists into his National Bloc, hoping to tame them, and so gave them 35 seats and respectability. The state also failed to stop the squads. From late 1920 they attacked socialist unions and councils in the Po valley and elsewhere, and the police and army often looked away. Finally, when the March on Rome came, Prime Minister Facta was ready to proclaim martial law, but the King refused to sign, and then invited Mussolini to form a government. The decision was not forced by the Fascists, whose several tens of thousands of poorly armed men could probably have been dispersed by the army.

The Fascists were nevertheless a real force. Mussolini had founded the movement in March 1919 and, by moving to the right in 1920, won the support of landowners and industrialists. The squads, led by local bosses such as Balbo and Farinacci, destroyed the Socialists' power in whole provinces, and in November 1921 the movement became the National Fascist Party with hundreds of thousands of members. The breaking of the general strike of August 1922 showed that they could do what the state could not. The March on Rome was a bluff but a successful one, because it created a threat that the King and politicians chose not to resist. Mussolini was also skilful: he combined violence with negotiation, and presented himself as a respectable leader who would restore order.

The conditions of the time created the opportunity. The mutilated victory, symbolised by the loss of Fiume, left nationalists bitter, and the unemployment and inflation after the war, together with the Biennio Rosso of strikes and factory occupations in 1919-20, frightened the middle classes and property owners, who turned to the Fascists as protection from socialism. Without these fears the squads would not have found sponsors.

The role of the elites links these factors. Landowners funded the squads, industrialists gave money, the Church was relieved to see the Socialists weakened, and the King, afraid of civil war and doubtful of the army's loyalty, thought that Mussolini would be easier to control inside a coalition. His first government included Liberals, Nationalists and Catholics, and only a few Fascists. Many of these men believed they could use him.

In assessing the factors, the weakness of the Liberals and the elites' decisions were necessary conditions, because a government that was determined and united could have defeated the March. But weakness was itself partly produced by the Fascist violence and by the fear of the left, and without the squads the establishment would have had no reason to turn to Mussolini. I therefore agree that weakness was the main reason, because the decisive act, the King's refusal to resist, was the choice of the establishment, but the Fascists' strength and tactics made that choice seem attractive. The two were interdependent, and it was the combination which brought him to office.

stem: 'Mussolini's government achieved more in propaganda than in practice.' Evaluate this view with reference to the economy, the Corporate State and foreign policy. [30]

points.description: Propaganda: the cult of the Duce, Minculpop, the press, radio, film, rallies, sport and architecture
Economy: the battles for the lira, grain and land; results and costs (Quota 90, dearer bread, the Pontine Marshes)

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The view contains a great deal of truth, because the image of a strong, modernising Italy was much more impressive than the results, but it is too sweeping, since some policies had real effects.

The propaganda was formidable. The press was controlled from the mid-1920s and the Ministry of Popular Culture took over the press, radio, film and the arts in 1937. The Duce was shown as sportsman, airman and infallible leader; the rallies, the architecture and sporting victories such as the World Cups of 1934 and 1938 gave an image of national revival. This made Mussolini genuinely popular for a time. Because the press was censored, failures could be hidden.

In the economy, the policies often had better effects in publicity than in practice. The Battle for the Lira brought the lira back to about 90 to the pound, a matter of prestige, but exports became dearer and wages were cut. The Battle for Grain raised wheat output and reduced imports, which was presented as a triumph, but land was diverted from fruit, olives and livestock, and bread became dearer. The Battle for Land drained the Pontine Marshes and founded new towns, which were widely publicised, but the area reclaimed was small, and the great estates of the south were untouched. Autarky in the later 1930s reduced imports, but Italy still depended on foreign coal, oil and metals. Living standards did not rise much.

Other policies had real consequences. In the Depression the state established the IMI in 1931 and the IRI in 1933, which took over failing banks' holdings in industry and gave the state a large share of Italian industry, an achievement that outlasted the regime. Public works created jobs, and the OND and welfare measures such as family allowances brought some benefits. The Lateran Treaties of 1929 settled the quarrel with the papacy and strengthened the regime. These were real achievements, although the Depression recovery was slow and unemployment remained high.

The Corporate State fits the view closely. It was presented as a new way of ending class conflict, with twenty-two corporations from 1934 and a Chamber of Fasces and Corporations in 1939. In practice independent unions and strikes were banned, employers kept control of wages and hiring, and the corporations had little real power. It served propaganda and control more than it achieved cooperation.

Foreign policy also had a gap between image and reality. Corfu in 1923, the protectorate over Albania and above all the conquest of Abyssinia in 1935-36 brought prestige and an empire, and Mussolini spoke of a new Roman empire. But the war cost money and led to sanctions and isolation from Britain and France, driving Italy into the Axis with Germany. The Pact of Steel of 1939 left Italy dependent on a partner it could not match, and in 1940 the army was ill-equipped. The gap between talk and military strength was shown by the defeats that followed.

Overall, the view is largely right about the Corporate State, the battles and foreign policy, where ambitions were not matched by results. It is less true of the IRI, the Lateran Treaties and the order the regime provided, which had substantial effects. I conclude that propaganda did indeed outdo practice in most areas, particularly in the economy for ordinary people and in foreign policy, but that the regime did achieve some real, lasting changes, so the view is true in general but overstated.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There is good evidence that the Fascist regime changed the surface of Italian life more than its substance, so the view is largely correct, but it overlooks real changes in the position of the Church and in the experience of young people.

Policy towards women shows the limits. The Battle for Births launched in 1927 aimed to raise the population, using a tax on bachelors, marriage loans, family allowances and prizes for mothers, and it banned contraception and abortion in 1930. It also restricted women's work, paid them less than men and limited their access to posts. Yet the birth rate continued to fall, as in other industrial countries, and many women had to work for economic reasons. The Fascist women's groups gave women organisation and training, but no political power. The policy strengthened a conservative view of women but did not reverse the long-term trend, so the evidence supports the view.

Policy towards young people had greater reach. The Gentile reforms of 1923 and later changes put religion in primary schools, imposed a single state textbook from 1930 and made university professors take an oath of loyalty in 1931. The ONB, founded in 1926, enrolled children by age for sport, drill and Fascist teaching, and by 1937 membership was effectively required. Millions of young people wore uniforms and went to camps, and some enjoyed opportunities that they would not otherwise have had. However, the effect on belief was limited. Many joined because membership helped at school or work, and families and the Church remained influential. By the time of the war many young people were disillusioned, and several later joined the partisans. The regime changed their activities more than their loyalties.

Religious policy produced the clearest change. The Lateran Treaties of 1929 created the Vatican City State, ended the quarrel since 1870 and, through the Concordat, made Catholicism the state religion, gave religious instruction in schools and gave church marriage civil effect. This changed the relationship between Church and state, and it gave the regime the support of millions of Catholics. Yet the changes strengthened the Church more than they transformed society: it kept its schools and Catholic Action, resisted the regime's attempt to control youth in 1931, and later was uneasy about the racial laws of 1938 and the alliance with Germany.

The wider picture also supports the view. The OND reached millions with leisure and cheap holidays, but participation was often for advantage and not conviction. Open opposition was small, with leaders imprisoned or exiled, such as Gramsci, Sturzo and the Rosselli brothers. Historians disagree about how far Italians consented, with some, such as De Felice, stressing real consent in the early 1930s and others stressing coercion and conformity. The south and the poor were affected little by most of these policies.

I therefore agree that Fascist policies changed Italian society less than the regime claimed: the birth rate, family life, regional differences and the independence of the Church show strong continuities. But the view should be qualified, since the youth organisations and schools changed everyday experience for a generation, and the Lateran Treaties altered the position of the Church in public life. The most accurate judgement is that the regime transformed the outward forms and institutions of Italian life but not the values and behaviour of most Italians.
